claims.text: Eutectic high-entropy alloys in the initial state have a dual-phase lamellar-colony structure with numerous internal boundaries.
A dual heterogeneous structure can comprise coarse grains, ultra-fine grains, and heterogeneous nanoprecipitates.
Introducing this dual heterogeneous structure into a eutectic high-entropy alloy can improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility.
The heterogeneous structure can relieve stress concentration during deformation.
Coherent heterogeneous nanoprecipitates can minimize elastic misfit strain at interfaces.
The dual heterogeneous structure provides alternative pathways for partial dislocations to glide.
Stress relief, reduced interfacial misfit strain, and alternative partial-dislocation pathways lead to enhanced ductility and strength.
The modified material will have greater strength than the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
The modified material will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline.
Defects or impurities introduced while producing the heterogeneous structure could compromise the material's properties.
The optimal composition and processing conditions for producing the dual heterogeneous structure are uncertain.
Controlled room-temperature tensile tests on modified and unmodified alloys can test the predicted strength and ductility changes.
The hypothesis is falsified if the modified material fails to improve both strength and ductility relative to the unmodified baseline.
